source.title: Understanding activation patterns in artificial neural networks by exploring stochastic processes: Discriminating generalization from memorization
source.authors: S. Lehmler; Muhammad Saif-ur-Rehman; T. Glasmachers; Ioannis Iossifidis

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears complete; no garbling or cut-off that affects this study was evident.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains image classifiers on natural and shuffled labels, then compares training and held-out accuracy. It also measures activation statistics against the train–validation accuracy gap, using a different method from the claim versions’ cited studies.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports accuracies for many widths, datasets, and training regimes; the rows below retain a bounded set of examples showing natural-label generalization and shuffled-label memorization. Table 2 reports activation statistics, while the text describes their relation to the generalization gap; the supplied text does not give numeric Figure 3 values.
record.test_reason: The study reports natural-label validation accuracy and shuffled-label training and validation accuracy in additional architectures and datasets, bearing on V1. Table 1 also compares convolutional and fully connected classifiers trained from scratch, bearing on V3. Its activation statistics do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that activation statistics can distinguish natural-label training from forced shuffled-label memorization in their experiments, with lower mean firing rates during memorization and weaker separation when earlier layers can memorize. They describe width and depth evidence as weak, acknowledge imperfect Poisson-model fit, and call for broader validation and studies of naturally occurring memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD with learning rate 0.1, momentum disabled, batch size 256, and a 10% validation split; compares original-label training with randomized-label memorization. This is not the exact cited study recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported activation-statistic differences vary with observed layer width and with whether all layers or only later layers are allowed to memorize; effects also vary by dataset and model. The authors describe width and depth evidence as weak.

fits_no_version.finding: Memorizing networks generally have lower mean firing rates and higher mean Fano factors. Differences depend on width and which layers can memorize, and can overlap in deeper networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Last-hidden-layer activation statistics distinguish forced shuffled-label memorization from natural-label training in these image classifiers, with dependence on architecture and training restrictions.

record.problems: The study observes only the last hidden layer and reports aggregated statistics. Some Table 1 models do not fully memorize randomized labels. The authors describe evidence for width and depth dilution effects as weak and call for broader validation. Figure 3 values are not numerically stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports additional widths, datasets, and MemRetrainLast and MemRandomLast conditions; these were not extracted due to the 60-row limit. Table 2 and Table 5 contain many per-model firing-rate and Fano-factor values, but they do not directly measure V7’s magnitude-aware sharpness. Figure 3 values are plot-only in the supplied text.

untested.parts: The original architectures and complete original recipes are not replicated. MemRetrainAll starts from natural-label trained weights, and DenseNet uses ImageNet pretraining. The study therefore does not establish the full comparison using identical initialization and training histories.
Although widths are swept, the one-hidden-layer MLPs do not reach zero natural-label training error. Training to convergence and behavior beyond their interpolation threshold are not established.

The causal contribution of local connectivity, learned sparse local connections, and initialization of fully connected networks from trained convolutional networks are not tested. CIFAR-100 and SVHN comparisons are absent.
No reported controlled comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.
No batch-size intervention or fixed-epoch comparison.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness measure or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
No influence-based identification and removal of memorized training examples.

missing.what: Explicit CNN-versus-MLP comparison rows for V3. MNIST CNN/MLP validation accuracies at widths 64, 128, 256 and 512 are respectively 98.50/97.10, 98.63/97.57, 98.62/97.62 and 98.70/97.95%. FashionMNIST pairs are 89.58/88.85, 91.63/98.28, 91.52/89.27 and 90.37/89.63%. Although additional accuracies were declared omitted, their bearing on V3 was missed entirely.

Verify the printed 98.28% FashionMNIST validation accuracy for MLP-128. It exceeds its 91.75% training accuracy and is markedly above neighboring MLP results; the supplied text gives no correction. This value determines the apparent reversed V3 comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text is an arXiv v1 manuscript; conclusions here apply to that text. Random-label induction is relevant to V1 because V1 explicitly concerns that experimental manipulation. The activation diagnostics themselves do not establish any supplied version. Additional Table 1 conditions already declared in rows_left_out are not separately listed as missing V1 results.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests MLPs, CNNs, and DenseNet121-based models on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10. It does not test Inception, AlexNet, or the exact Zhang et al. 2017 architectures and recipes.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep focused on test error past the interpolation threshold.
No matched comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks’ image test errors or learned local connections.
The study measures firing statistics, not magnitude-aware sharpness or the norm- and margin-based comparisons named in this version.
